title: Who Said Martial Law?
dek: The president will not rule an election emergency in or out. His allies are saying the words aloud. Here is what the Constitution, two centuries of statutes and the Supreme Court actually allow, and what they forbid.
body: On September 28, a reporter from TIME asked the president of the United States whether he would rule out declaring a state of emergency before the midterm elections, absent widespread violence in the streets. Donald Trump's answer, as printed in the magazine's transcript, was brief. "I don't rule anything out or in. We'll see. You mean the Insurrection Act?" Told yes, he went on: "No, I've never used it. I could use it. A lot of people think I should use it sometimes." Asked whether he planned to send immigration agents to polling places, he said he hadn't thought of it.

Two days later, on a video call streamed for election activists, a lawyer who has known the president since childhood said the quieter part plainly. Peter Ticktin, who represents former Colorado county clerk Tina Peters, told the audience that "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." In a later interview with Axios, he added that authorities would "probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment." Another participant, Gregory Stenstrom, said he wanted the election paused and proposed that the president invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run their elections.

Mr. Trump has not used the words "martial law" about the November 3 election. No order has been signed. The White House, asked about the call, said that Americans "deserve elections that are safe, secure, and transparent." It did not say whether the president would use emergency powers.

Sixteen days before the vote, then, the country finds itself in an unusual position. A president has declined to rule out an extraordinary step. People close to him are describing one. And the question of what he could lawfully do has moved from law-school seminars to county election offices. This is an attempt to answer it carefully.
## The words on the record

The context matters, because the October conversation did not begin in October. In January, the president told Reuters that "we shouldn't even have an election"; the White House said he was joking. In February, on Dan Bongino's podcast, he said Republicans "ought to nationalize the voting." Senate Majority Leader John Thune responded that fifty separate state systems are harder to compromise than one, and Speaker Mike Johnson defended state administration of elections.

The administration has also acted. In March the president issued an executive order directing the U.S. Postal Service to stop delivering mail ballots to voters who did not appear on lists submitted in advance by state officials. On September 1, the Department of Homeland Security began what it called a criminal voter-fraud surge in nine states, focused on alleged registration or voting by noncitizens. Washington is one of them. The people on the September 30 call included Ms. Peters, who was convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment and whose sentence Colorado's governor later commuted. She met with the president this month.

None of that is a declaration of anything. But a serious account has to hold two facts at once: no emergency has been proclaimed, and the head of the executive branch has publicly kept the option open.
## There is no martial law statute

Begin with the phrase itself. "Martial law" appears nowhere in the Constitution, and no federal statute authorizes a president to declare it. The Constitution's only reference to emergency suspension of ordinary legal protections sits in Article I, the article that describes Congress: the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus may not be suspended "unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it." The placement is not an accident of drafting. When President Lincoln suspended the writ on his own authority in 1861, Chief Justice Roger Taney, sitting as a circuit judge in Ex parte Merryman, wrote that the power belonged to Congress. Congress later ratified the suspension by statute in 1863.

The Supreme Court's defining statement on military rule over civilians came after the Civil War. In Ex parte Milligan, decided in 1866, the Court held that a civilian in Indiana could not be tried by a military commission while the civilian courts were open and functioning. Its central sentence has been quoted in every serious discussion of the subject since: "Martial rule can never exist where the courts are open, and in the proper and unobstructed exercise of their jurisdiction." The Court allowed that genuine necessity, such as an invasion that closes the courts, could justify military government in a theater of war. It refused to let necessity be presumed.

The principle survived a far greater emergency. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, the territorial governor of Hawaii declared martial law and the military took over the islands' courts. In Duncan v. Kahanamoku, in 1946, the Supreme Court held that the statute Congress had passed for Hawaii did not authorize military tribunals to try civilians for ordinary crimes once the immediate danger had passed. The Court wrote of the "traditional apprehensions about military rule" that run through American history.

Governors have tried martial law too, and courts have reviewed them. In 1932, in Sterling v. Constantin, the Court rejected the claim that the governor of Texas could use a martial law declaration to enforce limits on oil production beyond the reach of federal courts. Whether a claimed emergency justified the measures taken, the Court held, was a question the judiciary could examine.

The consistent lesson is that martial law in the United States is not a power any official holds by declaring it. It is, at most, a description of what happens when military force is used in conditions so extreme that civilian institutions have stopped functioning, and even then the courts have insisted on reviewing it afterward. On November 3, every federal and state court in the country will be open.
## The Insurrection Act and its limits

What does exist is a statute the president named himself. The Insurrection Act, now codified at 10 U.S.C. sections 251 through 255, descends from laws passed in 1792 and 1807, and was last substantively amended in 1874. It allows a president to use the armed forces, or to federalize a state's National Guard, in three circumstances. The first, section 251, applies when a state's legislature or governor asks for help suppressing an insurrection. The second, section 252, applies when "unlawful obstructions, combinations, or assemblages, or rebellion" make it impracticable to enforce federal law through ordinary judicial proceedings. The third, section 253, applies when violence or conspiracy deprives people of constitutional rights and state authorities cannot or will not protect them, or when it obstructs the execution of federal law.
Section 254 adds a formal step. Before using troops, the president must issue a proclamation ordering insurgents to disperse.

History shows what the act has been for. President Eisenhower invoked it in 1957 to send the 101st Airborne to Little Rock, after Arkansas's governor used the National Guard to keep Black students out of Central High School in defiance of a federal court order. President Kennedy used it in 1962 at the University of Mississippi and in 1963 in Alabama. President Johnson used it in 1965 to protect civil rights marchers in Selma. Its most recent use came in 1992, when California's governor asked President George H.W. Bush for troops during the Los Angeles riots. In its modern history, the act has been used most consequentially to enforce the rights of voters and citizens against state officials who refused to.

The courts have given presidents considerable latitude on the threshold question of whether an emergency exists. In Martin v. Mott, in 1827, the Supreme Court held that the president's judgment about when to call out the militia was conclusive on the officers who received the order. That deference is the reason legal scholars across the spectrum have long described the act as dangerously broad.

But the act has a structure, and the structure matters. It authorizes the military to execute the laws when ordinary enforcement fails. It does not authorize the military to suspend laws, and it says nothing about elections. The Brennan Center's Elizabeth Goitein and Sean Morales-Doyle, in an analysis published October 16, put it simply: the act lets presidents enforce the law, not violate it.
## The Posse Comitatus Act and the Illinois case

The default rule runs the other way. The Posse Comitatus Act, passed in 1878 as Reconstruction ended, makes it a crime to use the Army, and now the Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, to execute the laws "except in cases and under circumstances expressly authorized by the Constitution or Act of Congress." The Insurrection Act is the principal such authorization. Without it, soldiers do not police civilians.

The past year produced the first serious judicial tests of these rules in generations. In June 2025, the president federalized part of California's National Guard during immigration protests in Los Angeles under a different statute, 10 U.S.C. section 12406, which allows federalization when the president is "unable with the regular forces to execute the laws." California sued. On September 2, 2025, after a three-day trial, Judge Charles Breyer of the Northern District of California ruled that the deployment had violated the Posse Comitatus Act and enjoined the use of troops for civilian law enforcement in the state. The Ninth Circuit stayed that order pending appeal, and later upheld a separate order requiring federalized troops to leave Los Angeles. By December 31, 2025, the administration had ended its deployments in Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland.

The decisive ruling came from the Supreme Court on December 23, 2025, in Trump v. Illinois. By a vote of six to three, the Court refused to let the administration deploy federalized Guard troops in the Chicago area. The majority read "regular forces" in section 12406 to mean the active-duty military, not civilian law enforcement. That reading means a president must first be unable to execute the laws with the regular military before federalizing the Guard under that statute, and the majority added that the Posse Comitatus Act likely bars using active-duty troops in the first place absent an express exception. Justice Kavanaugh concurred on narrower grounds. Justices Alito and Thomas dissented, arguing that the Posse Comitatus Act should not limit the president's inherent constitutional authority. Justice Gorsuch dissented separately and called for further briefing on when the military may be used domestically.

Trump v. Illinois did not decide anything about the Insurrection Act. Its practical effect is to make that act the remaining statutory route for domestic deployment, which is one reason the president's answer to TIME drew such attention.
## The statute written for exactly this
Even if a president validly invoked the Insurrection Act, a separate body of law speaks directly to elections, and it was written for a crisis worse than any the country faces now.

Section 592 of Title 18 makes it a federal crime for any officer of the Army or Navy, or any other person in the civil, military or naval service of the United States, to order, bring, keep or have under his authority troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held, unless force is necessary "to repel armed enemies of the United States." The penalty is up to five years in prison and disqualification from holding any federal office of honor, profit or trust. Section 593 separately criminalizes interference with elections by members of the armed forces, and a civil provision, 52 U.S.C. section 10102, also prohibits it.

The history of section 592 is the heart of the matter. According to an analysis by Joseph Nunn of the Brennan Center, published October 8, the provision was enacted in early 1865, in the last months of the Civil War. Its principal sponsor, Senator Lazarus Powell of Kentucky, described it as a direct constraint on the president. Congress had watched federal troops in the border states screen voters, turn away citizens carrying opposition ballots and, in Kentucky, arrest opposition candidates, under orders that flowed from the war power. Missouri was under martial law from 1861 to 1865. Kentucky was under martial law during the 1864 election. Congress's response, in wartime, was to forbid the practice. In 1909, Congress revised the law and removed an exception that had allowed troops to "keep peace at the polls."

There is a contrary view inside the executive branch, and it should be stated. A 1968 opinion from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel asserted, in a few sentences, that section 592 does not apply once a president has invoked the Insurrection Act, on the theory that the prohibition was aimed at subordinate officers rather than presidents. The memo referred to a fuller opinion that has never been made public. Mr. Nunn and analysts writing at Lawfare argue that the reading is "exactly backwards," because the election statute is the more specific law, was revised after the Insurrection Act was last amended, and was enacted precisely to stop presidentially directed interference. No court has ruled on the question. But the burden would fall on anyone claiming that the law Congress wrote to keep soldiers away from ballot boxes during a civil war silently lapses in a lesser emergency.
## Congress sets the date, and the states run the vote
A president also lacks the power the September 30 call imagined most often: to pause, postpone or take over an election.

Article I, section 4 of the Constitution gives the "Times, Places and Manner" of congressional elections to the state legislatures, subject to laws passed by Congress. The president is not mentioned. Congress has exercised that power. Since 1872, federal law, now at 2 U.S.C. section 7, has fixed the election of representatives on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. Senate elections are held on the same day. Moving that date would require an act of Congress, signed into law. In 2013, in Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, the Supreme Court described the Elections Clause as a grant of authority to the states and Congress over the mechanics of federal elections. The Constitution assigns the executive no role in it.

Nor does the National Emergencies Act fill the gap. A presidential emergency declaration unlocks roughly 140 specific statutory powers, according to the Brennan Center's count, and none of them concerns elections. A draft executive order circulated in December 2020 proposed using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to seize voting machines; it was never issued, and the Brennan analysis argues that statute cannot be used to take American-owned property in which no foreign entity has an interest.

The constitutional framework for weighing such claims dates to 1952. When President Truman seized the nation's steel mills during the Korean War, citing his powers as commander in chief, the Supreme Court struck the seizure down in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer. Justice Robert Jackson's concurrence became the governing test. A president acting with Congress's authorization is at the height of his power. A president acting against it is at its weakest: "When the President takes measures incompatible with the expressed or implied will of Congress, his power is at its lowest ebb." Congress has set the election date, criminalized troops at the polls and assigned election administration to the states. A president who tried to override any of that would be acting at the lowest ebb Jackson described.
## The courts are already ruling

The country does not need to speculate about whether judges will review executive action on elections, because they are doing it. In June, Judge Indira Talwani of the District of Massachusetts found key provisions of the March mail-ballot order unconstitutional. After the Supreme Court lifted her first injunction on narrow procedural grounds in August, the Postal Service published a 95-page plan requiring states to submit voter lists through a new federal system. Judge Talwani blocked it again, calling it an unconstitutional attempt to take election powers from the states. On September 14, Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., ruled that the agency lacked authority to impose the rules. The same day, the Supreme Court left Judge Talwani's order in place for November, finding the administration "is unlikely to succeed on the merits." Justices Alito and Thomas dissented. Justice Kavanaugh, concurring, wrote that state and local officials did not have time to implement the rule before the election. Separately, a federal judge in Washington State permanently blocked the president's 2025 election executive order in a suit brought by Washington and Oregon.

The pattern matters for November. Courts can issue temporary restraining orders within hours. State and local officials, not federal ones, hold the ballots and run the count, and they are under no obligation to follow an order that has no basis in law.
## What the military says

The most important institutional answer has come from the military itself. In August, Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan wrote to the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, and to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, asking for written assurances. General Caine replied in a letter dated August 28. The Joint Force, he wrote, has "no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard" to polling places in 2026, and no plans to use them to seize ballots or voting machines. "I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order," he added, and he wrote that election administration and security "remain the fundamental responsibility of state and local officials." As of Senator Slotkin's August 31 release, Secretary Hegseth had not responded. His predecessors, the release noted, had given such assurances when asked.

Civilian federal agents are a separate question. In February, Heather Honey, the Department of Homeland Security's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity, told state officials there would be no ICE presence at polling locations. The department's secretary, Markwayne Mullin, has since said agents could appear if there is a threat or a warrant. Arizona's secretary of state said he could not take the February promise at face value. Section 592 covers armed federal agents as well as troops, which is why state officials have focused on the distinction.
## Washington's playbook

In this state, the preparation has been specific. On September 3, two days after the DHS surge began, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and Attorney General Nick Brown sent all 39 county election offices a guide titled "Election administration: a guide to federal and state authority." It tells county staff to verify the identity of any federal personnel, to determine whether a request is voluntary or backed by a subpoena or warrant, and to consult county counsel before agreeing to interviews or producing records. Documents should not be released on a verbal request, and ballot processing need not stop for one. If a judicial warrant is served, staff are not to obstruct agents, hide files, shut down computers or move documents; a county may designate someone to observe and photograph the search, request an inventory, and later seek the return of anything taken beyond the warrant's terms. The guide addresses a hypothetical federal attempt to seize voting equipment under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and the Insurrection Act, whose use to intimidate voters it calls "unprecedented."

Mr. Hobbs said he learned from news reports that Washington had been included in the DHS initiative. He has cited five documented fraud cases in the state between 2008 and 2025, out of about 90 million ballots. Mr. Brown said he had "no reason to believe this is a legitimate inquiry."

Washington law restricts out-of-state troops from entering without the governor's consent, except where federal law provides otherwise. If a president federalizes the Guard, the governor loses command of it. Gov. Bob Ferguson said in June 2025, after the California ruling, that the state would be prepared if the administration attempted a deployment here.

The state's strongest protection is structural. Washington votes entirely by mail. There are no traditional precinct polling places for most voters to be turned away from; ballots are mailed to every registered voter, returned through the Postal Service or county drop boxes, and counted by county election staff under state law and observation by both parties.
## What the law cannot do by itself

Every statute described here is a constraint written on paper. Its force depends on officials who honor it, courts that enforce it and a public that knows it exists. The legal case against military interference in the November election is unusually strong. It rests on the Constitution's assignment of election power to the states and Congress, on a Civil War statute written for this exact danger, on a Supreme Court that ruled against the administration on domestic deployment ten months ago, and on a Joint Chiefs chairman who has put in writing that he expects no unlawful order.

What the law cannot do is make the question go away. A president has said he will not rule it out. Men close to him have described commandeering ballots and voting machines. Election officials across the country have spent the autumn writing contingency plans for scenarios that had no precedent in modern American history.

In Washington, the practical instructions are simple. Ballots must be postmarked or placed in a county drop box by 8 p.m. on November 3. Voters who encounter interference can report it to their county elections office or the Secretary of State. And the law, on this point, is not ambiguous: no president can declare martial law, no soldier may stand at a polling place, and the date of the election belongs to Congress.

title: "We Turned Our Lights Off"
dek: A father of three died in a burning car after an ICE stop in Michigan. The agent on the 911 call couldn't say what the stop was for. It's the latest name on a list that keeps growing.
body: Sunday morning, September 20, on the southwest side of Grand Rapids, Michigan. ICE agents tried to pull over a car driven by Mario David Coronado Juarez, a Guatemalan construction worker in his 30s who sent money home to his wife, Macedonia, and their three kids. He didn't stop. He drove off, hit a tree, and the car caught fire. He died at the scene.

DHS says its officers immediately dropped the stop and weren't chasing him. They say they saw smoke from about half a mile away and ran back to help and fight the fire before local crews arrived. DHS also says the car was registered to someone else it considered removable.
On October 14, Michigan Public released the 911 call one of the agents made after the crash, obtained through a records request.
> We tried lighting a guy up and he wouldn't stop so we turned our lights off. (ICE agent, 911 call)
When the dispatcher asked what the stop was for, the agent said she'd have to ask her partner.

Grand Rapids police say they had no part in the stop and didn't know about it until the crash. Mayor David LaGrand says it's clear Mario fled from ICE agents, but that a lot of questions remain. He also wrote this: when government agencies cause harm instead of reducing it, they are worse than useless. At the city's request, and at Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's direction, Michigan State Police are investigating. Rep. Hillary Scholten wants to know whether agents had a warrant or any basis for the stop, and has asked ICE to preserve the body-camera and vehicle footage.
> What happened Sunday morning cannot go without justice being served. (Macedonia Juarez, his wife)
## The last fatal shooting

Coronado Juarez died in a crash, not a shooting. The most recent fatal shooting by an immigration agent on record is from July 13 in Biddeford, Maine. An ICE officer shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 25, a Colombian asylum seeker with a pending case and a work permit, on his way to a cleaning job. Bullets hit his 3-year-old daughter's car seat, which the Maine attorney general's office is holding as evidence. ICE says the officer fired fearing for public safety. His partner calls it murder.
## The tally

ABC News counted at least 21 people shot by federal immigration agents in Trump's second term as of late September, eight of them fatally, including three U.S. citizens. Other counts differ. October alone brought two more cases that weren't fatal: an ICE officer fired seven rounds into a car in Manhattan on October 8, hitting the driver in the neck with his 5-year-old son in the back seat, and an ICE SUV ran down a construction worker in Houston on October 10. Harris County's district attorney says that man was intentionally struck and run over. ICE denies it.
Then there are the deaths inside. Twenty-five people have died in ICE detention so far this year, after 31 in 2025. TIME reported in August that detention deaths had hit a 22-year high.
## Here at home

No one in Washington state has died at the hands of immigration agents in 2025 or 2026, as far as the public record shows. A June incident in Blaine left one person injured. But don't get comfortable. As we report elsewhere in this issue, immigration agents are still pulling Washington driver data despite state law.
Know your rights. Keep the hotline numbers in your phone. And if you see ICE, film from a safe distance. In this story, the video and the audio are the only reason we know what we know.
